title: Sagittarii et pueri equites
titleEn: The Archery Contest and the Boys' Ride — Aeneid V.485–579
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The games for Anchises go on with archery. Aeneas raises a ship's mast and hangs a dove from its top on a cord; four men draw lots from a bronze helmet. The first arrow strikes the mast, the second cuts the cord and the dove flies off, and the third brings her down dead from under a dark cloud, which leaves old Acestes with no prize to win. He shoots all the same, and his arrow bursts into flame high in the air and burns away like a falling star, a portent whose meaning, Virgil says, only the outcome taught. Aeneas takes it as a sign from heaven and gives Acestes the winner's honours and a mixing-bowl that once belonged to Anchises, and Eurytion, who really brought the bird down, bears it without envy. Then, with the contest not yet dismissed, Aeneas sends for Epytides, the guardian of his son Iulus, to tell the boy to lead out his troop of horsemen in honour of his grandfather, and the crowd clears the field. The boys ride in before their parents in three troops of twelve, each under a leader: little Priam, grandson of the old king, on a spotted Thracian horse; Atys, from whom the Roman Atii descend; and Iulus himself, the handsomest, on a horse Dido gave him. The Trojans see their own fathers' faces in them, and the part ends as Epytides gives the signal from far off and cracks his whip.
part: The Archery Contest and the Boys' Ride (V.485–579)

sentences.t:
Protinus Aeneas celeri certare sagitta
invitat qui forte velint, et praemia ponit,
ingentique manu malum de nave Seresti
erigit, et volucrem traiecto in fune columbam,
quo tendant ferrum, malo suspendit ab alto.
sentences.l:
At once Aeneas to contend with swift arrow
invites whoever by chance may wish, and sets out prizes,
and by a huge hand a mast from the ship of Serestus
raises, and a winged dove on a cord run across,
at which they may aim the iron, from the high mast hangs.
sentences.i: At once Aeneas invites any who care to try the swift-arrow contest and sets out prizes; with a mighty heave he raises a mast from the ship of Serestus, and from its high top hangs a winged dove on a cord drawn across, for the archers to aim their steel at.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the archery contest, a shoot at a dove tied to a mast, which Virgil takes from the funeral games of Homer's Iliad. 'Protinus' is 'at once'. 'Celeri certare sagitta' is 'to contend with swift arrow', 'certare' an infinitive after 'invitat' ('invites to…'), 'sagitta' an ablative of means. 'Qui forte velint' is a relative clause with the subjunctive, 'whoever may happen to wish', the antecedent ('eos') left out. 'Ponit' is 'sets out' (the Latin Library prints 'dicit', 'announces'). 'Ingenti manu' is an ablative of means: 'manu' is 'hand', though it can also mean 'band' of men. 'Seresti' is the genitive of 'Serestus', one of Aeneas's companions. 'Erigit' is 'sets upright'. 'Volucrem' is 'winged'. 'Traiecto in fune' is 'on a cord run across (the mast's top)'. 'Quo tendant ferrum' is a relative clause of purpose, 'at which they are to aim their iron', the subjunctive 'tendant' showing the purpose.

sentences.t:
Convenere viri, deiectamque aerea sortem
accepit galea;
sentences.l:
Came together the men, and the cast lot a bronze
helmet received;
sentences.i: The men gathered, and a bronze helmet took in the lots thrown into it;
sentences.n: 'Convenere' is 'convenerunt', the ending '-ere' for '-erunt' (you'll see this constantly). 'Sortem' is a singular for the lots, 'sors' used collectively; 'deiectam' is its perfect participle passive, 'cast down (into it)'. 'Aerea galea' is the subject of 'accepit': 'a bronze helmet received the lot'.

sentences.t:
et primus clamore secundo
Hyrtacidae ante omnes exit locus Hippocoöntis;
sentences.l:
and first, with favouring shout,
of the son of Hyrtacus before all comes out the place, of Hippocoon;
sentences.i: and with a shout of approval the first place, before all the rest, falls to Hippocoon, son of Hyrtacus;
sentences.n: 'Primus… locus' is 'the first place' in the order of shooting, decided by lot; 'exit' is 'comes out (of the helmet)'. 'Clamore secundo' is an ablative of manner: 'secundus' is 'favouring', 'applauding'. 'Hyrtacidae' is a genitive of the Greek type in '-ae' (a patronymic, 'son of Hyrtacus') in apposition to 'Hippocoöntis', both depending on 'locus': 'the place of Hippocoon, Hyrtacus's son'. The two dots in 'Hippocoöntis' show that 'oö' is two syllables.

sentences.t:
quem modo navali Mnestheus certamine victor
consequitur, viridi Mnestheus evinctus oliva.
sentences.l:
whom lately in the naval contest Mnestheus, victor,
follows, Mnestheus bound round with green olive.
sentences.i: Mnestheus, lately winner in the ship race, follows him, Mnestheus with his head wreathed in green olive.
sentences.n: 'Quem' is a connecting relative (you'll see this constantly): 'and him'. 'Modo' is 'just now'; 'navali… certamine' is 'in the naval contest', the ship race run earlier in this book. 'Victor' is in apposition to 'Mnestheus', 'the winner' of that race. 'Consequitur' is a deponent, 'follows (next)', and takes the accusative 'quem'. 'Mnestheus' is repeated for emphasis. 'Viridi… oliva' is an ablative of means with 'evinctus', the perfect participle passive of 'evincio', 'bound round', 'wreathed'.

sentences.t:
Tertius Eurytion, tuus, o clarissime, frater,
Pandare, qui quondam, iussus confundere foedus,
in medios telum torsisti primus Achivos.
sentences.l:
Third Eurytion, your, O most illustrious, brother,
Pandarus, who once, ordered to break the treaty,
into the midst you hurled a missile, first, of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: Third comes Eurytion, your brother, most renowned Pandarus, you who once, ordered to break the truce, were the first to hurl a weapon into the Greek ranks.
sentences.n: 'Tertius' is 'third', in the order of the draw. 'Tuus… frater' is held apart by 'o clarissime', and the name 'Pandare' waits for the next line: Virgil turns aside to speak to Pandarus (the great archer of the Trojan side, who in the Iliad broke the truce between the armies). 'Clarissime' is a vocative superlative. 'Qui… torsisti' is a relative clause whose verb is second person, agreeing with 'Pandare', 'you who hurled'. 'Iussus confundere foedus' is 'ordered to confound (break) the treaty'. 'In medios… Achivos' is 'into the midst of the Achaeans', 'medios' agreeing with 'Achivos' (a variant of 'Achaeos'), and 'primus' is predicative, 'first'.

sentences.t:
Extremus galeaque ima subsedit Acestes,
ausus et ipse manu iuvenum temptare laborem.
sentences.l:
Last, and at the helmet's bottom settled Acestes,
daring, he too, with the hand of young men to try the task.
sentences.i: Last, at the very bottom of the helmet, came Acestes, who, old as he was, dared to try with his own hand the labour of the young.
sentences.n: 'Extremus… subsedit' is 'settled last': his lot lay at the bottom of the helmet, so he draws last, and the verb is said of the man for his lot. 'Galea ima' is 'at the helmet's bottom', 'imus' agreeing with 'galea', an ablative of place with no preposition. 'Ausus' is the perfect participle of the semi-deponent 'audeo', 'having dared', with the infinitive 'temptare' (Greenough's spelling; the usual 'tentare'). 'Et ipse' is 'he too', 'even he'. In 'manu iuvenum… laborem' the likeliest reading is 'manu' as means ('with his hand') and 'iuvenum' depending on 'laborem' ('the young men's task'); the line frames 'laborem' at the end.

sentences.t:
Tum validis flexos incurvant viribus arcus
pro se quisque viri, et depromunt tela pharetris.
sentences.l:
Then with sturdy strength the curved bows they bend in
for himself each of the men, and draw out arrows from quivers.
sentences.i: Then each man, for himself, bends his curved bow with all his strength, and draws his arrows from the quiver.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Validis… viribus' is an ablative of manner, 'with strong strength'. 'Flexos' is 'curved', a perfect participle passive of 'flecto'; 'incurvant' is 'bend in', the archers bending the bows to string them. 'Pro se quisque viri' is 'each of the men for himself': 'viri' is the plural subject of 'incurvant', and 'quisque' ('each') stands in apposition to it. 'Depromunt' is 'bring out', and 'pharetris' an ablative of separation, 'from quivers'.

sentences.i: The first arrow, shot by the young son of Hyrtacus, goes through the sky with a whir of the string, cleaves the swift air, and sticks fast in the timber of the mast that faces it.
sentences.n: 'Prima' agrees with 'sagitta' and is set early; the arrow is the first because Hippocoon drew first place. 'Nervo stridente' is an ablative absolute, 'the string whirring' ('nervus' is literally 'sinew', so 'bowstring'). 'Hyrtacidae iuvenis' is two genitives, both with 'sagitta': 'of Hyrtacus's son, of the young man' (Hippocoon, 492); 'iuvenis' is here a genitive singular. 'Volucres… auras' is 'the winged breezes', a transferred epithet. 'Diverberat' is 'beats apart', 'cleaves'. 'Adversi… mali' is 'of the mast facing (it)', and 'arbore' (the wood) is an ablative of place with no preposition after 'infigitur', 'is fixed in'.

sentences.t:
Intremuit malus, timuitque exterrita pennis
ales, et ingenti sonuerunt omnia plausu.
sentences.l:
Trembled the mast, and feared, terrified in her wings,
the bird, and with huge applause rang all things.
sentences.i: The mast shuddered, and the frightened bird quivered in terror on her wings, and everywhere rang the roar of applause.
sentences.n: 'Intremuit' is the perfect of 'intremo', 'shuddered'. 'Timuit' is 'feared', and 'exterrita pennis' is 'terrified in her wings': 'pennis' is an ablative of respect, her fear showing in the flutter of her wings. The Latin Library prints 'micuitque', 'quivered', for 'timuitque'; either gives a bird in a flutter. 'Exterrita' is a feminine participle agreeing with 'ales', 'bird' (a winged creature, here the dove). 'Sonuerunt omnia' is 'all things resounded', 'ingenti… plausu' an ablative of means, 'with huge applause'.

sentences.t:
Post acer Mnestheus adducto constitit arcu,
alta petens, pariterque oculos telumque tetendit.
sentences.l:
Next keen Mnestheus took his stand, the bow drawn back,
seeking the heights, and equally eyes and missile stretched.
sentences.i: Next keen Mnestheus took his stand with his bow drawn back, aiming high, and strained eye and arrow alike toward the mark.
sentences.n: 'Post' is an adverb, 'next', 'afterwards'. 'Adducto arcu' is an ablative absolute, 'the bow drawn back'. 'Alta petens' is 'seeking the heights', 'aiming high', for the dove hangs high. 'Tetendit' is the perfect of 'tendo' and has two objects of different kinds, 'oculos telumque': a zeugma, 'stretched eyes and arrow' alike. 'Pariter' is 'equally', 'at once'.

sentences.t:
Ast ipsam miserandus avem contingere ferro
non valuit:
sentences.l:
But the bird herself, to be pitied, to touch with iron
he was not able:
sentences.i: But, poor man, he could not hit the bird herself with his steel:
sentences.n: 'Ast' is an old, poetic form of 'at', 'but'. 'Ipsam avem' is 'the bird herself', as against the cord. 'Contingere' is 'to touch', 'to hit', 'ferro' (an ablative of means) is the iron head of the arrow. 'Miserandus' is a gerundive used as an adjective, 'to be pitied', an exclamation of sympathy for Mnestheus. 'Non valuit' is 'was not able', perfect of 'valeo'. The colon leads to what he did hit.

sentences.t:
nodos et vincula linea rupit,
quis innexa pedem malo pendebat ab alto:
sentences.l:
the knots and the linen bonds he broke,
by which tied as to the foot she was hanging from the high mast:
sentences.i: he severed the knots and the linen cords by which she was tied by the foot and hung from the high mast:
sentences.n: 'Nodos et vincula linea' is 'the knots and the linen cords', 'linea' a neuter plural adjective with 'vincula'. 'Quis' is 'quibus', an ablative of means, 'by which'. 'Innexa' is the perfect participle passive of 'innecto', 'tied', agreeing with the bird (not named, but 'avem' in 509 and 'columbam' in 488 supply it); 'pedem' is an accusative of respect, 'tied as to the foot' (a use taken from Greek). 'Pendebat' is imperfect, 'was hanging'; 'malo… ab alto' is 'from the high mast', the noun comes first and the preposition 'ab' stands between it and its adjective. The colon leads to the bird's escape.

sentences.t: illa notos atque alta volans in nubila fugit.
sentences.l: she, to the south winds and into the lofty clouds flying, fled.
sentences.i: She flew off to the winds, up into the high clouds, and was gone.
sentences.n: 'Illa' is the dove. 'Notos' is the accusative plural of 'Notus', the south wind, so 'the winds'; it is a goal of motion with no preposition, in parallel with 'in nubila'. 'Alta… nubila' is 'the lofty clouds', where the Latin Library prints 'atra', 'dark', a change of sense, though both give a bird escaping into the sky. 'Volans' is a present participle, 'flying', and 'fugit' is 'fled' (the form could be present or perfect; the sense here is the perfect).

sentences.t:
Tum rapidus, iamdudum arcu contenta parato
tela tenens, fratrem Eurytion in Pota vocavit,
iam vacuo laetam caelo speculatus, et alis
plaudentem nigra figit sub nube columbam.
sentences.l:
Then swift, a while now on the bow made ready the drawn
missile holding, Eurytion his brother to his vows called,
and now in the empty sky the glad one having spied, and with wings
clapping, he pierces beneath a dark cloud the dove.
sentences.i: Then Eurytion, quick, who had long been holding his arrow drawn on the ready bow, called upon his brother in prayer; and, as soon as he spied the dove, glad in the now empty sky and beating her wings, he pierced her beneath a dark cloud.
sentences.n: The print has 'Pota' in 514, a misprint for 'vota', corrected here (the Latin Library reads 'uota', and the sense needs it). t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i read 'vota'. 'Rapidus' is 'quick', and 'iamdudum' 'for a good while now'. 'Arcu contenta parato tela tenens' is 'holding his arrow drawn on the ready bow': 'tela' is a plural for a single arrow, 'contenta' the perfect participle passive of 'contendo', 'drawn tight', and 'arcu parato' an ablative of place, 'on the bow made ready'. 'Fratrem… in vota vocavit' is 'called his brother into his vows', that is, invoked him in prayer; the brother is Pandarus (495). 'Speculatus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'speculor', 'having spied', with its object 'columbam', delayed to the end of the unit; 'laetam' is 'glad' (she is free of the cord) and 'vacuo… caelo' 'in the empty sky' an ablative of place. 'Alis plaudentem' is 'clapping with her wings', and 'nigra sub nube' 'beneath a dark cloud'.

sentences.t:
Decidit exanimis, vitamque reliquit in astris
aetheriis, fixamque refert delapsa sagittam.
sentences.l:
She fell lifeless, and left her life among the stars
of the sky, and carries back, gliding down, the fixed arrow.
sentences.i: She tumbled down lifeless, having left her life among the stars of heaven, and in falling brings back the arrow lodged in her.
sentences.n: 'Decidit… reliquit… refert' runs perfect, perfect, present: the present 'refert' is the vivid tense for the last picture. 'Exanimis' is 'lifeless'. 'In astris aetheriis' is 'among the stars of the upper air', a poetic height; she died under a cloud, but the line lifts the shot to the sky. 'Delapsa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'delabor', 'having glided down'. 'Fixam… sagittam' is 'the arrow lodged (in her)', with 'fixam' separated from its noun.

sentences.t: Amissa solus palma superabat Acestes;
sentences.l: The palm lost, alone remained Acestes;
sentences.i: With the prize beyond his reach, only Acestes was left;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Amissa… palma' is an ablative absolute, 'the palm (of victory) lost', that is, gone for him, since the three targets have been hit. 'Solus' is 'alone'; 'superabat' is imperfect, 'was left over', 'remained'.

sentences.t:
qui tamen aerias telum contendit in auras,
ostentans artemque pater arcumque sonantem.
sentences.l:
who yet his missile into the airy breezes sped,
showing both his art, the father, and his twanging bow.
sentences.i: Yet he sped his arrow up into the lofty air, the old man, to show both his skill and his ringing bow.
sentences.n: 'Qui tamen' is a connecting relative with 'tamen', 'who nevertheless': beaten before he starts, he shoots anyway. 'Telum contendit' is 'sent his missile', 'contendo' used of shooting. 'Aerias… auras' is 'the airy breezes', 'the high air'. 'Ostentans' is 'displaying'. 'Pater' is 'father', a respectful title for Acestes, set between the words of the pair 'artem… arcum', and 'artemque… arcumque' is the double '-que… -que' (you'll see this constantly), 'both his skill and his bow'. 'Sonantem' is 'twanging'.

sentences.t:
Hic oculis subito obicitur magnoque futurum
augurio monstrum;
sentences.l:
Here to the eyes suddenly is thrown, and for great
omen about to be, a portent;
sentences.i: Here a portent is suddenly thrown across their sight, one destined to be a great omen;
sentences.n: 'Hic' is an adverb, 'here', 'at this point'. 'Obicitur' is the present passive of 'obicio', 'is thrown in the way of', with the dative 'oculis'. 'Subito' is 'suddenly' (the Latin Library prints 'subitum', 'a sudden portent', almost the same sense). 'Futurum' is the neuter future participle of 'sum', agreeing with 'monstrum', 'about to be', and 'magno… augurio' is a dative of purpose, 'for a great omen'. 'Monstrum' is 'portent', a sign from the gods, from 'moneo', 'warn'. The semicolon leads on to what the portent was.

sentences.t:
docuit post exitus ingens,
seraque terrifici cecinerunt omina vates.
sentences.l:
taught afterwards the huge outcome,
and late the awe-inspiring seers sang the omens.
sentences.i: What it meant the outcome taught later, and the awe-inspiring seers sang their omens too late.
sentences.n: 'Docuit' is 'taught', with its object left unsaid: 'the great outcome taught (it) afterwards'; Virgil does not say here what the outcome was. 'Post' is an adverb, 'afterwards', and 'exitus ingens' 'the huge result'. 'Sera… omina' is 'late omens': 'sera' is a neuter plural set apart from its noun, and the lateness belongs to the seers' prophecy, now only after the event. 'Terrifici' is 'awe-inspiring', 'terrible', set apart from 'vates', and 'cecinerunt' is 'sang', 'foretold', the verb of prophecy. 'Vates' is the plural of 'vates', 'seer'.

sentences.t:
Namque volans liquidis in nubibus arsit harundo,
signavitque viam flammis, tenuisque recessit
consumpta in ventos, caelo ceu saepe refixa
transcurrunt crinemque volantia sidera ducunt.
sentences.l:
For flying in the clear clouds burned the reed,
and marked its path with flames, and thin it receded,
consumed into the winds, as, from the sky often unfastened,
run across and a hair drawing, flying, the stars.
sentences.i: For the shaft, flying through the clear clouds, burst into flame and marked its way with fire, and then dwindled thin into the winds, as stars so often wrenched from the sky run across it, flying, and drag a long train of light behind them.
sentences.n: 'Namque' is 'for', explaining why it was a portent. 'Harundo' is 'a reed', so 'an arrow' (shafts were made of reed); 'volans' is 'flying'; 'liquidis in nubibus' is 'in the clear clouds', 'liquidus' meaning 'clear', 'translucent'. 'Arsit' is 'took fire'; 'signavitque viam flammis' is 'and marked its way with flames'. 'Tenuis' is 'thin', predicative with 'recessit', 'faded away'; 'consumpta' is 'burned up', 'in ventos' 'into the winds'. Then a simile with 'ceu', 'just as': 'caelo… refixa' is 'unfastened from the sky', 'caelo' an ablative of separation and 'refixa' the neuter plural perfect participle passive of 'refigo', 'wrenched loose' as if nailed there, agreeing with 'sidera'. 'Saepe' is 'often'; 'transcurrunt' is 'run across'; 'crinem… ducunt' is 'draw a hair (of light)', and 'volantia sidera', 'flying stars', are shooting stars. The long sentence holds its verb of the simile, 'ducunt', to the end.

sentences.t:
Attonitis haesere animis, superosque precati
Trinacrii Teucrique viri;
sentences.l:
With stunned minds they stuck, and the gods above having prayed to,
the Sicilian and Trojan men;
sentences.i: The men of Sicily and of Troy stood fast in stunned amazement, and prayed to the gods above;
sentences.n: 'Haesere' is 'haeserunt', the ending '-ere' for '-erunt': 'stuck fast', 'were rooted to the spot'. 'Attonitis animis' is 'with thunderstruck minds', an ablative of manner. 'Superos' is 'the gods above', a noun from the adjective 'superus'; 'precati' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'precor', 'having prayed to', and takes the accusative. 'Trinacrii Teucrique viri' is the subject, held back to the end: 'Trinacrii' 'Sicilians', 'Teucri' 'Trojans'.

sentences.t:
nec maximus omen
abnuit Aeneas;
sentences.l:
nor the greatest the omen
refuses, Aeneas;
sentences.i: and Aeneas, the greatest of them, does not turn the omen away;
sentences.n: 'Nec… abnuit' is 'does not refuse': 'abnuo' is 'refuse by a shake of the head', so 'reject' the omen as ill-omened; Aeneas welcomes it as a sign from the gods. 'Maximus' is 'greatest', 'foremost', and 'Aeneas' comes last in the unit, a subject delayed.

sentences.t:
sed laetum amplexus Acesten
muneribus cumulat magnis, ac talia fatur:
sentences.l:
but the glad Acestes having embraced,
with gifts he heaps him, great ones, and such things speaks:
sentences.i: but he embraces the delighted Acestes and heaps him with splendid gifts, and speaks to him thus:
sentences.n: 'Amplexus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'amplector', 'having embraced', in an active sense, and 'laetum' is 'joyful'; 'Acesten' is the Greek accusative of 'Acestes'. 'Muneribus… magnis' is an ablative of means, and 'cumulat' is 'piles up'. 'Ac talia fatur' is 'and says such things': 'fatur' is the present of the deponent 'for', and 'talia' is the usual lead-in to a speech; the colon introduces it.

sentences.t: “Sume, pater;
sentences.l: “Take, father;
sentences.i: “Take it, father;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Sume' is the imperative of 'sumo', 'take'; its object is left to be understood (the gift is named at 535, 'hoc munus'). 'Pater' is a vocative, a respectful address to Acestes (compare 521). The opening mark begins Aeneas's speech, which runs to 538.

sentences.t:
nam te voluit rex magnus Olympi
talibus auspiciis exsortem ducere honores.
sentences.l:
for you wished the great king of Olympus
with such auspices, outside the lot, to take honours.
sentences.i: for the great king of Olympus willed that you, under such omens, should take your honours outside the lot.
sentences.n: 'Nam' gives the reason. 'Rex magnus Olympi' is 'the great king of Olympus', that is, Jupiter, 'Olympi' a genitive. 'Voluit te… ducere' is an accusative and infinitive after 'volo', 'wished you to take'. 'Talibus auspiciis' is an ablative of attendant circumstance, 'under such auspices' (the sign of the burning arrow). 'Exsortem' is 'outside the lot', agreeing with 'te': Acestes drew the last lot, and the honour is given outside the order of the lots. 'Ducere honores' is 'to take (away) honours', and 'honores' is 'prizes'.

sentences.t:
Ipsius Anchisae longaevi hoc munus habebis,
cratera impressum signis, quem Thracius olim
Anchisae genitori in magno munere Cisseus
ferre sui dederat monumentum et pignus amoris.”
sentences.l:
Of Anchises himself, the long-lived, this gift you shall have,
a mixing-bowl stamped with figures, which Thracian once
to Anchises my father as a great gift, Cisseus
had given to bear, a memorial of himself and pledge of love.”
sentences.i: You shall have this gift from Anchises himself, aged as he was: a mixing-bowl embossed with figures, which Thracian Cisseus once gave my father Anchises as a splendid present, to carry with him as a reminder of the giver and a pledge of his love.”
sentences.n: 'Ipsius Anchisae longaevi' is 'of Anchises himself, the long-lived', a possessive genitive with 'munus', 'this gift': the games honour Anchises, and the bowl was his. 'Habebis' is the future, 'you shall have'. 'Cratera' is the Greek accusative of 'crater', 'a mixing-bowl' (wine and water were mixed in it); 'impressum signis' is 'stamped with figures', 'signis' an ablative of means. 'Quem… Cisseus' is a relative clause whose subject, 'Cisseus', waits until 537; 'Thracius olim' is 'a Thracian, once'. 'Anchisae genitori' is a dative with 'dederat', 'to Anchises, my father'; 'in magno munere' is 'as a great gift'. 'Dederat' is pluperfect, and 'ferre' an infinitive of purpose, 'to bear', 'to keep'. 'Sui… amoris' is 'of himself… of love', 'sui' a reflexive genitive ('of himself', Cisseus), 'monumentum' 'reminder' (the Latin Library spells it 'monimentum'), 'pignus amoris' 'pledge of love'. Line 572 repeats this line with one word changed. The closing mark ends Aeneas's speech.

sentences.t:
Sic fatus cingit viridanti tempora lauro,
et primum ante omnes victorem appellat Acesten.
sentences.l:
Thus having spoken, he binds with green laurel his temples,
and first before all as victor names Acestes.
sentences.i: With these words he wreathes Acestes's brow with green laurel and hails him as winner before them all.
sentences.n: 'Sic fatus' is 'so having spoken', the perfect participle of the deponent 'for', with 'Aeneas' understood. 'Cingit… tempora' is 'binds the temples' (Acestes's), 'viridanti lauro' an ablative of means, 'with green laurel', where 'viridanti' is a present participle used as an adjective, 'growing green'. 'Primum ante omnes' is 'first, before all'; 'victorem' is predicative, 'as victor', after 'appellat', 'names', 'hails'. 'Acesten' is the Greek accusative of 'Acestes'. (The Latin Library prints 'omnis' for 'omnes' in 540, a spelling variant.)

sentences.t:
Nec bonus Eurytion praelato invidit honori,
quamvis solus avem caelo deiecit ab alto.
sentences.l:
Nor good Eurytion at the honour preferred begrudged,
though alone the bird from the sky he threw down, from on high.
sentences.i: Nor did good-hearted Eurytion grudge the honour set above his own, though he alone had brought the bird down from the sky.
sentences.n: 'Bonus Eurytion' is 'good', 'generous' Eurytion. 'Invidit' is the perfect of 'invideo', 'begrudged', which takes the dative 'praelato honori', 'the preferred honour': 'praelato' is the perfect participle passive of 'praefero', 'carried before', 'put above (his own)'. 'Quamvis' takes the indicative 'deiecit' here, as often in verse; 'although'. 'Solus' is 'alone', and 'caelo… ab alto' is 'from the high sky', 'deiecit' 'threw down'.

sentences.t: Proximus ingreditur donis, qui vincula rupit;
sentences.l: Next goes forward to the gifts, he who the bonds broke;
sentences.i: Next steps up to the gifts the man who broke the cords;
sentences.n: 'Proximus' is 'next'. 'Ingreditur' is 'steps forward', and 'donis' a dative of direction, 'to the gifts'. 'Qui vincula rupit' is 'he who broke the cords' (Mnestheus, 510), the antecedent left out. The men are named by their deeds, and these lines do not say what Eurytion's own prize is.

sentences.t: extremus, volucri qui fixit arundine malum.
sentences.l: last, he who with the winged reed fixed the mast.
sentences.i: and last the man who pierced the mast with his swift arrow.
sentences.n: 'Extremus' is 'last', and 'ingreditur' is understood from the line before (an ellipsis of the verb). 'Qui fixit… malum' is 'who pierced the mast' (Hippocoon, 504). 'Volucri… arundine' is 'with the winged reed', an ablative of means; 'arundo' is 'reed', so 'arrow', the word spelled 'harundo' in 525 (the Latin Library prints 'harundine' here, a spelling variant).

sentences.t:
At pater Aeneas, nondum certamine misso,
custodem ad sese comitemque impubis Iuli
Epytiden vocat, et fidam sic fatur ad aurem:
sentences.l:
But father Aeneas, the contest not yet dismissed,
the guard to himself and companion of beardless Iulus,
Epytides, summons, and into a faithful ear thus speaks:
sentences.i: But Father Aeneas, with the contest not yet ended, calls to him Epytides, the guardian and companion of beardless Iulus, and says to him in confidence:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'At' is 'but', a turn to the next matter. 'Nondum certamine misso' is an ablative absolute, 'the contest not yet dismissed' ('missus', from 'mitto', 'let go', 'ended'). The object, 'Epytiden', the Greek accusative of 'Epytides' ('son of Epytus'), waits for 547, with 'custodem… comitemque' in apposition. 'Impubis Iuli' is 'of beardless Iulus', 'impubis' a genitive singular of 'impubes'; Iulus is Ascanius, the boy son of Aeneas. 'Ad sese' is 'to himself'. 'Fidam ad aurem' is 'to a faithful ear', the preposition between adjective and noun: he speaks in confidence.

sentences.t:
“Vade age, et Ascanio, si iam puerile paratum
agmen habet secum, cursusque instruxit equorum,
ducat avo turmas, et sese ostendat in armis,
dic ”ait.
sentences.l:
“Go on, and to Ascanius, if already a boyish
troop he has ready with him, and has drawn up the courses of horses,
let him lead out for his grandfather his squadrons, and show himself in arms,
tell,” he says.
sentences.i: “Go, and tell Ascanius, if he already has his troop of boys ready with him and has drilled the horses' courses, to lead out his squadrons in honour of his grandfather and show himself in arms,” he says.
sentences.n: The print has 'dic ”ait.' with no comma after the closing mark, a missing mark of punctuation (rule 5). t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i supply the comma ('tell,” he says') and close the speech after 'tell'. 'Vade age' is 'go, come then', 'age' an interjection. 'Et Ascanio… dic' is 'and tell Ascanius': the imperative 'dic' is held back to the end of the speech, over three lines, while the dative 'Ascanio' ('to the person told') comes first. 'Si iam puerile paratum agmen habet secum' is 'if he already has his boyish troop ready with him', 'habet paratum' ('has ready', a perfect participle with 'habeo') being the first step towards the Romance perfect. 'Cursusque instruxit equorum' is 'and has drawn up the horses' courses', the evolutions of the display described next. The commands are subjunctives of indirect command after 'dic': 'ducat… ostendat', 'let him lead… let him show', 'avo' a dative of interest, 'for his grandfather', Anchises, whose games these are.

sentences.t:
Ipse omnem longo decedere circo
infusum populum, et campos iubet esse patentes.
sentences.l:
He himself the whole from the long ring to withdraw
the poured-out people, and the fields orders to be open.
sentences.i: He himself bids the whole crowd, spread over the long course, withdraw from it, and the field lie open.
sentences.n: After the speech the narrator takes over: 'Ipse' is Aeneas himself. 'Iubet' governs two accusatives with infinitives: 'omnem… populum decedere', 'the whole people to withdraw', and 'campos esse patentes', 'the fields to be open'. 'Longo… circo' is 'from the long ring', an ablative of separation, the circus being the course; 'infusum' is the perfect participle passive of 'infundo', 'poured out', 'spread around', agreeing with 'populum'. (The Latin Library prints 'patentis' for 'patentes', a morphological variant only.)

sentences.t:
Incedunt pueri, pariterque ante ora parentum
frenatis lucent in equis, quos omnis euntes
Trinacriae mirata fremit Troiaeque iuventus.
sentences.l:
Advance the boys, and equally before the faces of their parents
on bridled horses gleam, whom all as they go,
of Trinacria having admired, murmurs, and of Troy, the youth.
sentences.i: The boys advance, and shine on their bridled horses before their parents' faces, and the whole youth of Sicily and of Troy murmurs in wonder as they pass.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the boys' ride begins. 'Incedunt' is 'march in', 'advance'. 'Pariter' is 'equally', 'together'; 'ante ora parentum' is 'before the faces of their parents'. 'Frenatis… in equis' is 'on bridled horses', the preposition between adjective and noun, and 'lucent' is 'gleam'. 'Quos omnis euntes… mirata fremit… iuventus' is 'whom, as they go, all the youth… wondering at, murmurs': 'omnis' can be the nominative singular, 'all the youth' (taken here), or Greenough's spelling of the accusative plural 'omnes', 'them all', agreeing with 'quos… euntes'; 'mirata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'miror', 'having marvelled at', in an active sense, with 'quos' as object; 'fremit' is singular with the collective noun 'iuventus', which comes last. 'Trinacriae Troiaeque' are genitives, 'of Sicily and of Troy'. (The Latin Library's 'euntis' for 'euntes' is a morphological variant only.)

sentences.t: omnibus in morem tonsa coma pressa corona;
sentences.l: To all, in custom, the hair trimmed is pressed by a wreath;
sentences.i: All wear their hair trimmed in the old fashion, pressed down by a wreath;
sentences.n: The print has 'omnibus' with a small letter after the full stop at the end of 555, a misprint for 'Omnibus', corrected here. t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i begin with a capital. 'Est' is left out. 'Omnibus' is a dative of reference, 'on all'. 'In morem' is 'according to custom'. 'Tonsa coma' is 'trimmed hair', 'tonsa' the perfect participle passive of 'tondeo'; 'pressa corona' is 'pressed by a wreath', 'pressa' the perfect participle passive of 'premo', 'corona' an ablative of means.

sentences.t: cornea bina ferunt praefixa hastilia ferro;
sentences.l: cornel-wood, two each, they carry, tipped, the spears, with iron;
sentences.i: each carries two cornel-wood spears tipped with iron;
sentences.n: 'Cornea' is 'of cornel-wood' (a hard wood good for shafts), 'bina' the distributive 'two each', and 'hastilia' is 'spears', 'shafts', all three agreeing, the noun last. 'Praefixa… ferro' is 'fitted in front with iron', 'tipped with iron', 'ferro' an ablative of means. 'Ferunt' is 'carry'.

sentences.t: pars levis umero pharetras;
sentences.l: a part, light on the shoulder, quivers;
sentences.i: some carry light quivers on the shoulder;
sentences.n: 'Pars' is 'some', a collective noun used in the sense 'some of them', with the verb 'ferunt' left out from the line before. 'Levis' is the accusative plural (Greenough's '-is' spelling) agreeing with 'pharetras', 'light quivers'. 'Umero' is 'on the shoulder'.

sentences.t:
it pectore summo
flexilis obtorti per collum circulus auri.
sentences.l:
goes on the top of the breast
pliant, round the neck, a hoop of twisted gold.
sentences.i: and on the upper breast, around the neck, runs a pliant circlet of twisted gold.
sentences.n: 'It' is the present of 'eo', 'goes', 'runs', with the subject 'circulus' coming last. 'Pectore summo' is 'on the top of the breast', an ablative of place. 'Flexilis' is 'pliant'; 'obtorti' is the perfect participle passive of 'obtorqueo', 'twisted round', and 'auri' 'of gold', so 'a bendable hoop of twisted gold', a torque. 'Per collum' is 'around the neck'.

sentences.t:
Tres equitum numero turmae, ternique vagantur
ductores:
sentences.l:
Three, in number of riders, are the squadrons, and by threes range
leaders:
sentences.i: The riders make three squadrons, and three captains ride at large:
sentences.n: 'Tres equitum numero turmae' is 'three squadrons in number of riders': 'equitum' is the genitive plural of 'eques', 'numero' an ablative of respect, 'turmae' 'troops of cavalry', and 'sunt' is left out. 'Terni' is the distributive 'three each', used for 'three' with a plural noun: 'three leaders', one for each troop. 'Vagantur' is 'range about', 'move freely'. The colon leads to the boys who follow them.

sentences.t:
pueri bis seni quemque secuti
agmine partito fulgent paribusque magistris.
sentences.l:
boys twice-six each following
in a divided column gleam, and with matching masters.
sentences.i: Twelve boys follow each leader, and gleam in their column parted into three, with leaders to match.
sentences.n: 'Bis seni' is 'twice six', 'twelve', 'seni' the distributive 'six each'. 'Quemque secuti' is 'following each (leader)', 'secuti' the perfect participle of the deponent 'sequor', with active sense, and 'pueri' the subject. 'Agmine partito' is 'in a column divided', an ablative of manner, 'partito' the perfect participle passive of 'partio'; 'fulgent' is 'gleam'. 'Paribusque magistris' is 'and with matching leaders', an ablative of attendant circumstance: the three captains match the three troops.

sentences.t:
Una acies iuvenum, ducit quam parvus ovantem
nomen avi referens Priamus,—tua clara, Polite,
progenies, auctura Italos,—quem Thracius albis
portat equus bicolor maculis, vestigia primi
alba pedis frontemque ostentans arduus albam.
sentences.l:
One troop of the young, which leads, exulting, little
Priam, his grandsire's name bearing — your famous, Polites,
offspring, to increase the Italians — whom a Thracian, with white
carries horse, two-coloured with spots, the tracks of the foremost
white foot and his forehead showing, lofty, white.
sentences.i: One troop of the young, which little Priam leads in glad triumph, bearing his grandfather's name, your famous offspring, Polites, who is to add to the Italians; a Thracian horse carries him, two-coloured with white spots, showing the white hoof of its forefoot and a white blaze on its lofty brow.
sentences.n: 'Una acies iuvenum' is 'one battle-line of the young', the first of the three troops. 'Ducit quam… Priamus' is 'which Priam leads': 'quam' is a feminine accusative relative, and 'ovantem', 'exulting', agrees with it. 'Parvus' is 'little': he is a boy. 'Nomen avi referens' is 'bearing his grandfather's name', 'avi' the grandfather, old King Priam. 'Tua clara, Polite, progenies' is 'your famous offspring, Polites', between dashes: a turn to the dead father, a vocative. 'Auctura Italos' is 'destined to increase the Italians', the future participle active of 'augeo' with the accusative: this Priam's line will add to the Italian stock. 'Quem… equus' is 'whom a horse carries'; 'Thracius… equus bicolor' is 'a Thracian horse, two-coloured', and 'albis… maculis' 'with white spots', an ablative of quality, split by 'bicolor' and 'portat'. 'Vestigia primi alba pedis' is 'the white marks of the front foot', object of 'ostentans', with 'frontem… albam', 'a white forehead'; 'arduus' is 'lofty', 'high-headed', predicative.

sentences.t:
Alter Atys, genus unde Atii duxere Latini,
parvus Atys, pueroque puer dilectus Iulo.
sentences.l:
The second Atys, from whom drew their race the Atii, Latin,
little Atys, and by the boy a boy beloved, Iulus.
sentences.i: Second comes Atys, from whom the Latin Atii trace their line, little Atys, a boy loved by the boy Iulus.
sentences.n: 'Alter' is 'the second' of the three leaders (the third is Iulus himself, 570). 'Atys' is a Greek nominative. 'Genus unde Atii duxere Latini' is 'from whom the Latin Atii drew their stock': 'unde' is 'from whom', 'genus' the object of 'duxere' (= 'duxerunt'), and the 'Atii' are the Roman family Atia, here traced back to a Trojan boy. 'Parvus Atys' is 'little Atys', the name repeated. 'Pueroque puer dilectus Iulo' is 'a boy loved by the boy Iulus': 'dilectus' is the perfect participle passive of 'diligo', 'loved', with 'Iulo' a dative of the agent, and 'puero… puer' set side by side.

sentences.t:
Extremus, formaque ante omnis pulcher, Iulus
Sidonio est invectus equo, quem candida Dido
esse sui dederat monumentum et pignus amoris.
sentences.l:
Last, and in form before all beautiful, Iulus
on a Sidonian horse was carried in, which fair Dido
had given to be of herself a memorial and pledge of love.
sentences.i: Last, and the most beautiful of all in form, Iulus rode in on a Sidonian horse, which radiant Dido had given him to be a keepsake of herself and a pledge of her love.
sentences.n: 'Extremus' is 'last'; 'est invectus' is 'was carried in', 'rode in', the passive of 'inveho' in its sense of riding. 'Forma ante omnis pulcher' is 'beautiful in form before all': 'forma' is an ablative of respect, and 'omnis' an accusative plural, Greenough's spelling of 'omnes'. 'Sidonio… equo' is 'a Sidonian horse', Sidonian meaning Phoenician, so from Dido's Carthage. 'Quem candida Dido esse sui dederat monumentum et pignus amoris' is 'which fair Dido had given to be her keepsake and pledge of love': 'esse' is an infinitive of purpose after 'dederat', and 'sui' a reflexive genitive, 'of herself'. The last line is 538 with 'ferre' changed to 'esse'. 'Candida' is 'bright', 'fair'.

sentences.t:
Cetera Trinacrii pubes senioris Acestae
fertur equis.
sentences.l:
The rest, the youth of Sicilian, of the elder Acestes,
is carried on horses.
sentences.i: The rest of the Sicilian youth, the followers of aged Acestes, ride on horseback.
sentences.n: 'Cetera… pubes' is 'the rest of the youth', 'pubes' a feminine noun with a collective sense, which the neuter plural 'cetera' follows by sense. 'Trinacrii… senioris Acestae' is 'of Sicilian, elder Acestes': both adjectives agree with the Greek-form genitive 'Acestae' (the Latin Library prints 'Trinacriis'; the sense stays 'Sicilian'). 'Senioris' is a comparative, 'older', 'aged'. 'Fertur equis' is 'is borne on horses', 'rides', 'equis' an ablative of means. 'Fertur equis' is a half-line: Virgil left some lines unfinished (the 'hemistichs', about 58 in the poem), and Greenough prints it short.

sentences.t:
Excipiunt plausu pavidos, gaudentque tuentes
Dardanidae, veterumque adgnoscunt ora parentum.
sentences.l:
They receive with applause the timid, and rejoice, watching,
the Dardanids, and of old parents recognise the faces.
sentences.i: The Trojans, glad as they watch, greet the anxious boys with applause, and in their faces recognise the faces of their forefathers.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Excipiunt' is 'receive', 'welcome'. 'Pavidos' is 'trembling', 'anxious', the boys; 'plausu' is an ablative, 'with applause'. 'Gaudent… tuentes' is 'rejoice, looking on', 'tuentes' the present participle of 'tueor'. 'Dardanidae' is 'the Dardanids', 'the Trojans' (descendants of Dardanus), put late as the subject. 'Veterum… parentum' is 'of the old forefathers', and 'adgnoscunt ora' 'recognise the faces' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library prints 'agnoscunt'): they see in the boys the faces of their forefathers.

sentences.t:
Postquam omnem laeti consessum oculosque suorum
lustravere in equis, signum clamore paratis
Epytides longe dedit insonuitque flagello.
sentences.l:
After the whole gathering, glad, and the eyes of their own
they had passed over on their horses, the signal, with a shout, to the ready
Epytides from far gave, and resounded with the whip.
sentences.i: When they had gladly ridden round the whole assembly and past the eyes of their own people, Epytides gave the ready boys the signal from afar with a shout, and cracked his whip.
sentences.n: 'Postquam… lustravere' is 'after they had surveyed': 'postquam' takes the perfect indicative, 'lustravere' is 'lustraverunt' (the ending '-ere' for '-erunt'), and 'lustro' is 'pass in review', 'survey'. The object is 'omnem consessum oculosque suorum', 'the whole seated gathering and the eyes of their own (kin)'; 'laeti' is 'glad', the boys, and 'in equis' 'on their horses'. 'Signum clamore paratis… dedit' is 'gave the signal with a shout to the ready ones', 'paratis' a dative of the person and 'clamore' an ablative of means; 'Epytides' is 'son of Epytus', and 'longe' 'from afar'. 'Insonuit flagello' is 'resounded with the whip', that is, cracked it, 'flagello' an ablative of means. The part ends as the signal is given, before the evolutions begin.
